title: Hagar names God (Genesis 16)
hook: a runaway servant meets an angel at a spring and calls God "the God who sees me"

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzedakah, counted to Abram for believing, under a sky of stars.

Ten years in the land, and still no child. So Sarai does something that is hard to hear today. She gives her Egyptian servant, Hagar, to Abram, hoping for a child through her. Hagar conceives, and the household cracks. Hagar looks down on Sarai. Sarai treats her harshly. And Hagar, pregnant and alone, runs away into the desert, on the road to Shur. She stops at a spring of water in the wilderness, and there, the Torah says, an angel of the LORD finds her. In a big, rich household, she is the foreign servant, the one nobody asks. And she is the one the angel comes looking for.
screen: `TEN YEARS, NO CHILD.` → `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.` → `AN ANGEL FINDS HER.`

segments.voice: The angel speaks first, and the first word is her name. In the old JPS translation: "Hagar, Sarai's handmaid, whence camest thou? and whither goest thou?" Notice this: in the whole chapter, Sarai and Abram never once say her name. They call her my handmaid, thy maid. The angel is the first to call her Hagar. Then the hard part. The angel tells her to go back to her mistress. Readers have struggled with that, and some commentators, like Nachmanides, said openly that Sarai did wrong in afflicting her, and Abram did wrong in allowing it. But the angel also gives her a promise of her own: a son, and many descendants. Call him Ishmael, the angel says, which means God hears, because God has heard your affliction. Then Hagar does something remarkable. She gives God a name of her own: El Roi. "Thou art a God of seeing," in the JPS wording: the God who sees me. The spring gets a name too: Beer-lahai-roi, the well of the Living One who sees me. A servant nobody named is named by an angel. A woman nobody listened to is told that God heard her. And the one nobody saw names God as the one who sees. Her son's name means God hears; her name for God means God sees. In one chapter, a servant with no power at all is given both.
screen: `THE ANGEL SAYS HER NAME.` · `A HARD COMMAND, A PROMISE.` · `ISHMAEL — GOD HEARS.` · `EL ROI — GOD WHO SEES ME.` · then, large: `THOU ART A GOD OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Picture one person you pass every day without really seeing: the person who cleans the office, the cashier, the bus driver, the quiet kid in the group chat, the neighbor you only know by their dog. See their face as clearly as you can, and ask yourself whether you know their name. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer; if not, just see them, fully, for a minute.
El Roi. The God who sees me: Hagar's name for God. That's the sixth week: Babel, lech lecha, midrash, Egypt, Lot's choice, the stars, and El Roi.
Your line: you are seen. Hagar was, at a spring in the desert. Six weeks, done.

screen: `DAY 42 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE STRANGERS AT THE TENT.`

howItsDone: Jews read Hagar's story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and her name for God, El Roi, the God who sees me, is often taught as a reminder to notice people who are overlooked.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 16:8 and 16:13 ('Thou art a God of seeing').

Claims: Hagar is the first person in the Torah visited by an angel, and the only person in the Torah to name God. Both are common in commentary; confirm (the angels at the garden are cherubim, not a visit).
Claim that Sarai and Abram never say Hagar's name in chapter 16 (they say 'my handmaid' 16:2, 16:5; 'thy maid' 16:6): confirm.
Nachmanides on 16:6: Sarai sinned in afflicting Hagar and Abram in permitting it, and God heard her affliction. Paraphrased; confirm.
Surrogacy through a servant is described as 'a known custom in that world'; confirm the framing.
